title: Hayden Panettiere’s Mom Blasts Gayle King and Megyn Kelly’s Criticisms of Her in Wake of Daughter’s Death
full_text: × Skip to main content By Carly Thomas Plus Icon Carly Thomas Senior Editor, Digital carly_thomas_ Follow Sign Up View All August 23, 2026 2:31pm Hayden Panettiere, Jansen Panettiere and Lesley Vogel in 2019. Amanda Edwards/Getty Images Lesley Vogel, Hayden Panettiere ’s mom, is slamming both Gayle King and Megyn Kelly for their recent criticisms in the wake of her daughter’s death . “I was very, very hurt and deeply disappointed in the lack of professionalism, the lack of compassion in slamming someone who’s lost two children, without even a modicum of consideration,” Vogel said during a recent interview with the Daily Mail regarding the CBS Mornings host and podcaster’s separate comments. “No one reached out to me before,” she added. “It’s shameful. It’s unconscionable to me.” Related Stories Movies Anna Paquin and Melissa Gilbert Call for Protection of Child Actors After Hayden Panettiere's Death: "Where Is the Collective Outrage?" News Hayden Panettiere's Boyfriend Gave Her Narcan Before Death, Brother Says The Hollywood Reporter has reached out to CBS Mornings for comment, but did not hear back at the time of publication. Panettiere, an actress known for her roles in Heroes , Nashville and the Scream franchise, died last Sunday at age 36. Following her death, Vogel spoke to NBC News on Tuesday, where she criticized her daughter’s on-again-off-again boyfriend Brian Hickerson and felt her daughter “lost her way.” “This person in her life that we have been trying to get rid of for quite some time was with her at her death and that was Brian Hickerson,” she said at the time. “I think Hayden was an amazingly talented person in so many departments and I think young people who grow up in the entertainment industry — it is a struggle and it’s a very challenging industry and it’s not unusual for them to sadly find the wrong path.” Vogel added, “I think Hayden sadly lost her way and I wish it were different. I wish she had stayed true to herself because she had many incredible attributes.” The following day, during Wednesday’s CBS Mornings broadcast , King criticized Vogel for focusing too much on her daughter’s struggles amid her death. “You know, guys, you read this and all I can think is, ‘Thanks, mom, for nothing,'” the host said. “It makes me so sad of the opportunity that you have after your daughter’s death that that’s what you choose to leave us with,” King added. As for Kelly, the former Fox News reporter went on The Megyn Kelly Show and declared, “You failed at your job… You got an F as a parent,” referring to Vogel. “You made a bunch of money off of your daughter,” Kelly added. “You probably have a super nice car and a big house. You failed. You raised someone to the age of majority who doesn’t feel safe, loved, or cherished. You’re a loser.” Panettiere had been open about her estranged relationship with her mother , who also served as her manager when she was growing up in the industry. In her memoir, This Is Me: A Reckoning , the actress detailed the pressure she felt from Vogel. During an interview with THR in May , Panettiere also opened up about the challenges of delving into her childhood and relationship with her mom when writing This Is Me . “Having to touch on everything about my relationship with my mother, that was one of the harder things to talk about,” Panettiere said. “While writing it, I realized even more so how much of a toll it took on me.” Page Six reported in May that Vogel had chosen the “no-contact route” with Panettiere after “20 years of trauma” and on the advice of professionals. Her son and Panettiere’s younger brother also died in February 2023 at the age of 28. THR

title: Shelley Fabares, Star of ‘The Donna Reed Show’ and ‘Coach,’ Dies at 82
full_text: Skip to main content By Cheryl Cheng , Duane Byrge August 23, 2026 1:27pm Shelley Fabares Michael Buckner/Getty Images Shelley Fabares, the wholesome daughter on The Donna Reed Show who went on to star opposite Elvis Presley in three movies and as Craig T. Nelson’s independent wife on Coach , has died. She was 82. Fabares died Saturday in Los Angeles after a brief illness, her family announced. Survivors include her husband, M*A*S*H actor Mike Farrell, whom she married in 1984. “To her family and friends, Shelley was a source of love, strength, laughter and comfort,” they said in a statement. “She was a devoted wife, cherished stepmother, daughter, sister, niece, aunt, family member and loyal friend whose warmth, generosity, humor and grace made an enduring difference in the lives of everyone who knew her. She had a remarkable ability to make people feel welcomed, valued and cared for.” Related Stories Movies Nick Glennie-Smith, Composer on 'The Rock,' 'The Man in the Iron Mask' and 'Secretariat,' Dies at 74 Movies Leslie Parrish, Actress in 'Li'l Abner' and 'The Manchurian Candidate,' Dies at 90 On the original One Day at a Time , Fabares played against her prim, good-girl persona as Francine Webster, a nasty business rival of Bonnie Franklin ‘s Ann Romano. (Her late aunt, Caesar’s Hour and The Band Wagon star Nannette Fabray , also appeared on the CBS sitcom, playing the mother of Franklin’s character.) Fabares also portrayed the wife of doomed Chicago Bears running back Brian Piccolo ( James Caan ) on the landmark 1971 ABC telefilm Brian’s Song . On The Donna Reed Show , which aired on ABC for eight seasons, from September 1958 through March 1966, Fabares played high schooler Mary Stone opposite Reed as her mom, homemaker Donna Stone; Carl Betz as her pediatrician dad, Dr. Alex Stone; and Paul Petersen as her younger brother, Jeff. When Mary left for college at the start of the sixth season, the Stones adopted a daughter, Trisha (Patty Petersen, real-life sister of Paul). Capitalizing on her national fame, Fabares — backed by Darlene Love and the Blossoms and Glen Campbell on guitar — recorded a version of “Johnny Angel,” which went to No. 1 on the Billboard Hot 100 in April 1962. She had debuted the song on a Donna Reed episode a couple months earlier. “I literally cannot sing. So there’s a lot of overdubbing,” she admitted in a 1983 interview. “The girls in the back — ‘Could you sing a little louder please?’ It was unusual. But [ The Donna Reed Show ] was very successful at that time, so [the song] had a built-in audience.” During “live” performances — in “the days when they would play the record and you would lip sync” — she recalled, “my worst experience was [when] I did a live local television show and, needless to say, the record stuck. I think I went into a coma.” Fabares starred on the ABC comedy Coach for eight seasons while earning a pair of Emmy nominations for playing Christine Armstrong, a TV newscaster and the girlfriend and then wife of Nelson’s college football coach, Hayden Fox. “Clearly, Christine is a very successful woman and firmly entrenched in her career and loves her work. And she loves this man,” she said . “It’s a difficult problem in life to find your balance. We’re all going through the same things. I have a wonderful relationship with my husband, but I’m still a career woman.” In 2015, NBC developed a Coach revival in which Nelson’s character returns to coaching and Fabares’ character is killed off, but the reboot did not emerge beyond the pilot stage. Michele Ann Marie Fabares was born in Santa Monica on Jan. 19, 1944. Her mother, Elsa, got her into modeling at age 3, and that led to TV appearances. By the time she was 9, Frank Sinatra was singing “Young at Heart” to her on an NBC special. She also appeared on a 1955 NBC adaptation of Our Town that starred Sinatra, Paul Newman and Eva Marie Saint and with Rock Hudson in Never Say Goodbye (1956). In 1958, she was on the ABC series Annette , which starred lifelong friend Annette Funicello . Fabares said Reed “was not given credit for being the head of her own series, the guiding force behind the series,” she said in 1994. “She produced the series, had an enormous part in writing it and also had four children at home. Having been there, I knew the amazing strength of that woman.” During a 2011 reunion of the show’s surviving castmembers, Fabares remembered when she was feeling nervous about having to dance during a scene. Reed tried to calm her down. “Shelley, there are three things I can’t do: I can’t swim, I can’t dance, and I can’t act.” But she had to do all three for a film scene. “Oh yeah, that movie I was talking about was It’s a Wonderful Life .” After several years as Mary Stone, Fabares concentrated on the big screen and appeared in the fun-in-the-sun movies Ride the Wild Surf (1964) with Fabian and Hold On! (1966) with Peter Noone of Herman’s Hermits. She then co-starred with Presley in Girl Happy (1965), Spinout (1966) — Betz played her dad in that one too — and Clambake (1967). “The first day of shooting [ Girl Happy ], I’m on the set. Something was happening, and I didn’t know what it was,” she said . “And I looked over, and it was Elvis. He was walking in. He wasn’t doing anything. He was just walking in. The presence that this man had … you couldn’t talk. Nobody did anything. You just sort of stopped. And I remember thinking, ‘Oh, my God. It’s Elvis Presley. I’m never going to be able to open my mouth around him.’ ” In the late 1960s, during a time of protest and rebellion, her good-girl appeal fell out of sync with the cultural zeitgeist. It wasn’t until Brian’s Song that she regained her career momentum. Buoyed by that role, Fabares rebounded to work on such popular series as The Brian Keith Show , The Practice with Danny Thomas and Highcliffe Manor . In the late ’70s and early ’80s, she starred on One Day at a Time , then showed a saucier dimension as the tart-tongued Eleanor Major on the syndicated soap opera spoof Forever Fernwood . Fabares also had guest-starring roles on Mannix ; Love, American Style ; Daniel Boone ; McCloud ; Mork & Mindy ; and Hello, Larry (as McLean Stevenson’s ex-wife). She had a liver transplant in October 2000 after spending nearly two years on the waiting list to receive one. In 1984, she married Farrell at Aunt Nanette’s Pacific Palisades home. The two had first met in 1970 when she was a guest star on Farrell’s series The Interns , but it was not until they reunited 12 years later during a CBS press tour that they started to date. (Earlier, Fabares had been married to record producer Lou Adler, while Farrell’s first wife was actress Judy Farrell , who played Nurse Abel on M*A*S*H .) Farrell, known to be a serious human rights activist, said his wife made him a bit more light-hearted. “People talk about how much more fun I am,” he said in 1991. “Shelley has allowed people to understand I’m not this unapproachable doomsayer.” Added Fabares: “Nothing in Mike’s life is casual. He’s very serious. Mike grounds me, and I think I pull him out sometimes. It’s a nice mix.” Shelley Fabares and Mike Farrell. Courtesy Fabares/Farrell family Survivors also include her stepchildren, Erin and Michael. THR

title: Anna Paquin and Melissa Gilbert Call for Protection of Child Actors After Hayden Panettiere’s Death: “Where Is the Collective Outrage?”
full_text: × Skip to main content By Carly Thomas Plus Icon Carly Thomas Senior Editor, Digital carly_thomas_ Follow Sign Up View All August 23, 2026 12:55pm Hayden Panettiere Dimitrios Kambouris/Getty Images Anna Paquin , Christy Carlson Romano and Melissa Gilbert are calling on Hollywood to protect child actors following the deaths of Hayden Panettiere , Michelle Trachtenberg and Daveigh Chase . Panettiere’s death at age 36 last Sunday prompted the three actresses, who were child stars themselves, to take their concerns public. Trachtenberg died at 39 in February 2025, while Chase died in July at age 35. “It’s not a coincidence that so many former, specifically pre-sexualized female, child ‘stars’ have profoundly sad lives and untimely ends. We were not as protected by the ‘systems’ that look great on paper, as we are supposed to be,” Paquin wrote on Instagram Friday. She rose to fame at 11 years old with her film debut in 1993’s The Piano , which earned her an Oscar for best supporting actress. Related Stories Movies Busan Film Festival Sets 23 Titles for Vision Korea, Vision Asia Sections General News Hayden Panettiere's Mom Blasts Gayle King and Megyn Kelly's Criticisms of Her in Wake of Daughter's Death “RIP HP, MT, DC and too many others. It’s a strange small club we belong to and you are worthy of support no matter how our industry makes us feel,” Paquin continued. “Literally DM me. I believe you and I will stand by your side. You aren’t alone. Let’s have each other’s backs. It might make public disclosure less terrifying.” The True Blood alum added in a separate post , “One more thing– As an adult I’ve had the pleasure of working on productions where the welfare and mental health of young performers was handled incredibly carefully. Especially around material that was intense. It is possible to holistically look after the kids on set and tell complex and sometimes upsetting stories. It just has to be the top priority of the production.” Earlier in the week, Elle published an essay by Romano — who appeared in 1996’s Everyone Says I Love You as a child before becoming a teen Disney star with her role in Even Stevens and voicing Kim Possible — where she compared child stardom to the degenerative brain disease chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE). “The former child actor exists in a category the world does not know how to hold. We are children when the public wants to feel protective of us, professionals when the industry wants to profit from us, and spoiled celebrities when we eventually show symptoms of having been both,” Romano wrote in part. “Early fame is like CTE. Not as a diagnosis. As a way of thinking about repeated impact. We now have language for youth sports: protocols, helmets, parents worried about concussions. But we have almost no language for what happens when stress, scrutiny, rejection, adult pressure, and the collapse of privacy become the architecture of a childhood. She added, “Young performers are still treated as exceptions. Lucky exceptions. Cute exceptions. Talented exceptions. Exceptions whose labor powers one of the most profitable storytelling machines in the world, while their mental needs are treated as inconvenient or irrelevant. Social work be damned.” Gilbert also shared a lengthy post on Substack Saturday, where she asked, “Why are these three sweet, wildly talented, vibrant, vital young women gone?” Gilbert landed her breakout role at just nine years old, playing Laura Ingalls Wilder on Little House on the Prairie from 1974 to 1983. “I did not know Hayden personally and only worked briefly with Mishy and Daveigh. It feels personal because I was them,” Gilbert wrote. “We are all members of the same tribe; Female Former Child Performers, and when one of us dies, it runs through all of us like an electrical current. When three of us die so close together, something is very, very wrong. We all know the stories of how the entertainment industry uses, abuses, exploits and then throws away it’s youngest, but for some reason, this trend is getting worse.” She later added, “Where is our Union in all of this? Where is the collective outrage? Where are the regulations? Where is the protection of privacy?” “It really seems like no one cares enough to enact real change. At least, not until the next death and everyone talks about how sad they are and how we must do something and then they forget and get on with their lives until it happens again and again and again,” Gilbert continued. “Yes, addiction is a real disease. Family dysfunction is real. PTSD is real. In actors, all those things are assets. They enable us to access emotion and share it with an audience. But when it comes through children, it should be treated tenderly, protectively, respectfully and in a way that is as limited as possible.” Gilbert’s post comes as her husband, Timothy Busfield, awaits trial in Albuquerque, New Mexico, after being accused of child sex abuse on the set of the former Fox/Warner Bros. Television series The Cleaning Lady . Gilbert has defended Busfield , who has denied the allegations. Panettiere started working in Hollywood at a young age, appearing in the soap opera One Life to Live at just four years old before starring in 2000’s Remember the Titans at 10, among other projects. As for Trachtenberg, she appeared in the Nickelodeon series The Adventures of Pete & Pete as a child, as well as 1996’s Harriet the Spy and 1999’s Inspector Gadget . Chase was known for voicing Lilo in 2002’s Lilo & Stitch when she was younger as well as starring in the 2002 horror film The Ring . THR

title: There Are Scores of Great New Animated Shows. The Emmys Won’t Nominate Them.
full_text: × Skip to main content By Steven Zeitchik Plus Icon Steven Zeitchik Senior Editor, Technology and Politics View All August 23, 2026 11:30am From left: Long-running shows like The Simpsons, South Park and Bob’s Burgers dominate the Emmys’ animated category. Illustrated by Brian Taylor One of the great creative innovations America has given the world in the past 30 years is TV animation. That sounds like hyperbole, but it’s true. The Simpsons changed how we look at the American family (and current events). Rick and Morty changed how we looked at comedy and the tragedy behind it. (“Wubba lubba dub dub.” Also, current events.) South Park changed how we looked at each other (and current events). The problem is that those shows all started doing that a very long time ago. Rick and Morty is nine seasons in. South Park is 28. The Simpsons is 37 damn seasons deep. There are children who weren’t born when the series debuted who now have children who themselves are old enough to think Bart has got this whole life thing figured out. Related Stories Hollywood Flashback Before 'The Pitt,' There Was 'St. Elsewhere' 'Awards Chatter' Podcast Emmy Nominee Patrick Ball on His Rollercoaster Journey to 'The Pitt' and How His Own Addiction Battle Has Informed His Performance All three of those shows are nominated for outstanding animated program this year. So is Bob’s Burgers , which just completed its 20th season. Now, a charitable view would hold that such shortlisting reflects the durability of these shows — how they manage to maintain their creative spark through so many changing winds. There is something to that — it’s not easy to do anything well for three decades, let alone maintain character freshness. But I fear the fact that animated characters don’t age — and that they’re basically money-minting machines for a few networks (especially Fox) — has led us to a pretty calcified place. No show should so regularly take a place on the Emmys stage. The Simpsons and Bob’s Burgers have been nominated every year since the Obama days. Nothing is that good for that long. What isn’t on the animated shortlist this year? Dark sci-fi like Owen Dennis’ Among Us on Paramount+. The acquired taste but still bold stylings of Raphael Bob-Waksberg’s time-jumping family series Long Story Short on Netflix. Joe Cappa’s Adult Swim single-dad delight Haha, You Clowns . These are all newish shows from the past year or two with great energy and original takes. But to look at the Emmys noms is to not even know they exist (and indeed, many viewers won’t without the exposure). A little breath of fresh air in the category comes via Smiling Friends , Adult Swim’s truly wacky take on a nonprofit and what it means to do good/be happy. And while I would hardly call anything in the George Lucas-verse fresh in 2026, Star Wars: Visions at least uses varied artists and styles in a way that feels original. But these shows seem token-y amid the Simpsons and South Park oak trees and probably won’t win anyway. What can the Emmys do to fix this? Fortunately, there are a few things. For starters, stop with just nominating a single episode. Unlike TV Academy convention elsewhere, the Emmys don’t award a show — they award an episode. That means that the kind of newer, zanier material that takes months to really settle into is completely disadvantaged — you’re not going to appreciate something weird and new if you just try to watch one episode. You’re just going to go back to something you know and like, such as The Simpsons or South Park . Of course, the irony is that The Simpsons and South Park were themselves once oddball and required a multi-episode commitment to appreciate. But now that they are appreciated, voters just keep rubber-stamping them. I mean, Rick and Morty hasn’t really been good in several years. But voters just keep checking the box without thinking there might be a new Rick and Morty waiting out there. The other irony is that many of the characters on these very shows would hate this kind of lazy legacy thinking and would balk at it. A category that is literally designed to celebrate subversiveness champions the sclerotic. Another fix: Stop with the international ghettoizing. My colleague David Canfield just covered this on the live-action side, but it applies on the animated side, too. Bluey is one of the best shows on television these past 10 years. And many people in America watch it. Find a way to make it eligible for the primetime Emmy. While we’re on the topic of Bluey , get rid of the “Eligibility in animation is for programming that targets an audience age 13 and above” rule. This is just not how people watch television anymore. And finally, open up the Phase II voting beyond just the animation branch to the whole TV Academy. Animation is one of two realms that has this limitation. And it’s having a bad effect. People in the animation branch work in the field, which means they tend to vote for the shows of folks they know or have worked with. So we get the 30-year veterans. I get why this exclusionary voting rule was first drafted: Animation is a specialized craft, and specialists should vote on their specialty. Also, there is a fear that the, ahem, unwashed masses who don’t work in animation won’t really know the shows because they’re too busy watching the live-action stuff. But if that was ever true, it’s not anymore. Everyone watches everything. All of these might seem like big changes, hard to implement, but they’re really not. They’re possible and would make a world of difference. And if you doubt it, there’s a group you can ask that will help. A group that looked at the world as it is and said, “Maybe there’s another, more daring way to view it.” They are, of course, called animators. title: ‘Tucci in Italy’ Cinematographer Matt Ball on Making Italy Look Delicious
full_text: × Skip to main content By Matthew Jacobs Plus Icon Matthew Jacobs thrnews@thr.com View All August 23, 2026 11:00am Says director of photography Matt Ball: “The work of making Tucci in Italy look beautiful has been done for me already.” National Geographic/Matt Holyoak (3) Tucci in Italy is swarming with handsome images: a mouthwatering dollop of spaghetti and clams inspired by a Neapolitan chef’s 94-year-old mother, majestic Renaissance-era palaces and quaint villages where the show’s host, Stanley Tucci , enlists locals to expound on Italian culture. But director of photography Matt Ball isn’t always looking for polish — he wants candor. “It’s not necessarily a show about how beautiful everything looks,” Ball says. “The primary goal is to get authenticity. And then we shoot around it and try to make it look as nice as we can.” Related Stories Hollywood Flashback Before 'The Pitt,' There Was 'St. Elsewhere' 'Awards Chatter' Podcast Emmy Nominee Patrick Ball on His Rollercoaster Journey to 'The Pitt' and How His Own Addiction Battle Has Informed His Performance Ball’s cinematography led to one of the three Emmy nominations that Tucci in Italy received this year, alongside a sound mixing citation and outstanding hosted nonfiction series or special. He met Tucci as a camera operator on Stanley Tucci: Searching for Italy , which ran for two seasons on CNN. When National Geographic picked up the retitled version, Ball was brought on as DP. They’re currently in production on another spinoff, this time set in Great Britain. Before shooting, Tucci, producer Lottie Birmingham and their research team map out a roughly seven- to 10-day stint in each city being featured that season. They find cooks, farmers, food producers and culinary experts to show off the region’s cuisine and landscapes. Ball, who collaborated with two camera operators and two assistants on Tucci in Italy , then designed shots as unobtrusive as possible so the contributors could feel comfortable. “The work of making it look beautiful has been done for me already,” Ball says, downplaying his aptitude for capturing the vistas of Sicily, Tuscany or Sardinia so elegantly. If Searching for Italy prioritized major destinations such as Rome and Milan , Tucci in Italy sought out less touristy locales, like Ball’s personal favorite stop, Le Marche. There, at the seaside restaurant Da Emilia, Tucci tried a spaghetti and mussels dish the chef’s eponymous grandmother had taught her to make years earlier. The Devil Wears Prada actor dined with the chef at a long outdoor table overlooking the Adriatic Sea — an example of the charisma that Ball encountered everywhere he went. “It looked fantastic,” he says. “The light was coming off the water, and it was a beautiful day. It was really lovely.” Ball, for his part, gets to sample many of the dishes, too. Some of that intake depends on how much offal, for example, he’s willing to eat. Ball’s food-oriented résumé is accidental, though. It started with a gig as a camera operator on the long-running Barefoot Contessa , where he met his wife. He’s since shot Be My Guest With Ina Garten as well as shows with celebrity chefs Jamie Oliver and Lorraine Pascale. He says he’ll stay on with Tucci as long as Tucci wants to continue his savory travels. “Everywhere we go,” he says, “you’ll always hear somebody whisper, ‘That’s Stanley Tucci!’ ” This story first appeared in an August stand-alone issue of The Hollywood Reporter magazine. title: Simon Wiesenthal Center CEO Calls Out Mark Ruffalo’s Paramount Remarks: “Obsession and Demonization”
full_text: × Skip to main content By Carly Thomas Plus Icon Carly Thomas Senior Editor, Digital carly_thomas_ Follow Sign Up View All August 23, 2026 9:44am Mark Ruffalo and Paramount. Amy Sussman/Getty Images; Justin Sullivan/Getty Images Jim Berk, CEO of the Simon Wiesenthal Center , is defending Paramount after the studio called Mark Ruffalo’s anti-merger comments “antisemitic.” “Words matter, and so does the willingness to draw a line when legitimate debate gives way to antisemitic tropes,” Berk wrote. “We commend Paramount for speaking clearly and refusing to allow prejudice to masquerade as political or corporate criticism. At a time when antisemitism is too often minimized, rationalized or repackaged in more socially acceptable language, this kind of moral clarity matters.” “Invoking Israel in an issue where it is completely irrelevant is a textbook case of obsession and demonization. Paramount was right to call it out. More leaders and institutions should have the courage to call antisemitism what it is, regardless of who is spreading it,” his statement concluded. Earlier this week, the Oscar-nominated actor, who has been an outspoken opponent of Paramount’s $111 billion deal for Warner Bros., highlighted Larry Ellison’s (Paramount CEO David Ellison’s father) Oracle’s ties to the Israeli military amid the Israel-Gaza war. Ruffalo resurfaced a clip from 2024 of former Oracle chief Safra Catz talking about “profoundly scary technologies” the tech company had built in relation to Israel’s war effort in Gaza. The actor also described the war as a “genocide” that “was built on an apartheid system of oppression powered by Oracle.” In response, Paramount clapped back , calling the Marvel star’s remarks “antisemitic.” The studio’s spokesperson’s statement read in part, “We are, as always, troubled when antisemitic tropes are invoked in purported service of a business dispute. Words like ‘genocide’ and ‘apartheid,’ applied to a corporate transaction, aren’t just wrong — they’re a bridge too far, and they cheapen the very real suffering those words are meant to describe. This doesn’t deserve a response in kind — and to be clear, we don’t tolerate prejudice of any kind, against anyone.” Creative Community for Peace, a Hollywood-based pro-Israel advocacy organization, has also called for Hollywood to boycott Ruffalo until the actor “retract[s] these remarks and apologize[s],” the group’s executive director, Ari Ingel, wrote in a statement. “ Mark Ruffalo ’s rhetoric has increasingly crossed the line from criticism of Israel into extremist and antisemitic messaging,” Ingel also wrote, adding, “Point blank, he has been warned before about the consequences of this rhetoric, yet continues contributing to the toxic antisemitic atmosphere we are witnessing today. That makes him culpable. His argument increasingly fuses hostility toward Israel and Zionism with Jewish-associated wealth, media ownership, oligarchic power and ominous warnings about concentrated control into a single narrative. Those echoes are impossible to ignore.” On Saturday, Ruffalo took to X to dismiss Paramount’s claims that his comments were “antisemitic” as well as offer a distinction between his criticism of the Israeli military and his views about Jewish people. He wrote in part, “The accusation that I am antisemitic is appalling and fundamentally dishonest. Criticizing the actions of the Israeli prime minister, a military technology contract or the executives who supply it is not the same as criticizing Jewish people. This critical and necessary dialogue is then dishonestly framed as being anti-Israel.” THR
